My data

The Fairness dataset is the ACS Income NC dataset from Fairlearn. Each row represents one person, and the dataset contains 5,000 rows. The data is based on American Community Survey information. The Sports dataset is the 10 MLB Pitchers 2015–2019 dataset. Each row represents one pitch, and the dataset contains 33,289 rows. It contains information about pitch types, pitch results, and release speeds.

put_in_place("fairness.csv", "data/tidy")
put_in_place("sports.csv", "data/sports")

fairness <- read_csv("data/tidy/fairness.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sports <- read_csv("data/sports/sports.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

if (looks_damaged(fairness) || looks_damaged(sports)) {
  stop("One of your data files looks damaged (each row in one column): it ",
       "may have been re-saved by a spreadsheet app. Ask your instructor ",
       "for a fresh copy.", call. = FALSE)
}

# PART A · FAIRNESS ==========================================================

# A0 · Your group and your outcome ------------------------------------------
# Session 1, slide 17: "My outcome is ___. My group is ___."
# YOUR TURN: replace "replace me" with your group column (no quotes), and
# FALSE with a TRUE/FALSE condition for your outcome. Examples (use YOUR
# columns; the Guided Project page lists them for every class dataset):
#   group = sex,           has_outcome = income == ">50K"
#   group = age,           has_outcome = readmit_30_days == 1

Part A · Fairness

My group: sex My outcome: income >= 50000

Question A: “Of each sex (group), what share has at least $50,000? (outcome)?” Question B: “Of everyone with an income of at least $50,000 (outcome), what share is each sex? (group)?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = sex,
    has_outcome = income >= 50000
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  group  has_outcome     n
  <chr>  <lgl>       <int>
1 Female FALSE        1776
2 Female TRUE          654
3 Male   FALSE        1473
4 Male   TRUE         1097

A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)

I predicted that males would have a higher rate of income above $50,000 than females. The plot allows me to compare the percentage of each group that reaches this income level. Each bar represents its own group’s total, making it possible to compare groups fairly even when they have different numbers of people.

A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)

The standard error ranges show how much uncertainty there is around each group’s estimated rate. A smaller group will generally have a wider range because it has fewer observations. This helps readers recognize that smaller groups are still important and should not be ignored when comparing outcomes.

A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group      n
  <chr>  <int>
1 Male    2570
2 Female  2430
a3_start <- min(a3_table$n) / 2

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor
[1] 1.054475
show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)

The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 1.1.

The original plot shows the full difference in group sizes starting from zero. The zoomed plot makes the difference easier to see but can make it appear larger than it really is. The filtered plot removes part of the scale and can be misleading because it hides some of the original data. I would publish the original plot because it shows the group sizes without exaggerating the difference.

A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)

Question A compares the percentage within each sex, while question B compares how much each sex contributes to everyone who meets the income outcome. The results can point in the same direction, but they measure different things because the groups may have different sizes. Question A is the better choice when comparing income rates between groups.

Part B · Sports

My group, outcome and value: My group is pitch_type, my outcome is result == “S”, and my numerical value is release_speed.

B0 · My group, outcome and value

b_data <- sports %>%
  mutate(
    group = pitch_type,
    has_outcome = result == "S",
    value = release_speed,
  )

b_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

B1 · The rate within each group

b1 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of pitches", y = NULL,
       fill = "Strike")

show_plot(b1)

The plot shows the percentage of pitches that resulted in strikes for each pitch type. Shares are more useful than raw counts because some pitch types may have been thrown much more often than others.

B2 · A mean with its two spreads

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Average pitch speed", y = NULL)

show_plot(b2)

The plot compares average release speeds across pitch types. Standard deviation describes how spread out individual pitch speeds are, while standard error describes the uncertainty in each group’s estimated mean. Comparing the means and these ranges helps show whether the differences between pitch types are meaningful.

B3 · Zoom or filter?

b3_table <- b_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
b3_table
# A tibble: 12 × 2
   group     n
   <chr> <int>
 1 FF    13681
 2 SI     4632
 3 CH     4488
 4 SL     3867
 5 CU     3436
 6 FC     2783
 7 KC      307
 8 IN       47
 9 <NA>     39
10 EP        5
11 FA        2
12 PO        2
b3_start <- min(b3_table$n) / 2

b3_counts <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

b3_zoom <- b3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)),
                  expand = FALSE)
b3_filter <- b3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)))

b3_lie_factor <-
  ((max(b3_table$n) - b3_start) / (min(b3_table$n) - b3_start)) /
  (max(b3_table$n) / min(b3_table$n))
b3_lie_factor
[1] 1.999854
show_plot(b3_zoom)
show_plot(b3_filter)

The zoomed plot makes differences between pitch counts easier to see, while the filtered plot removes part of the data from view. A reader could think that the differences between pitch types are larger than they actually are. My sports dataset does not have a year, season, or date column available for this analysis, so I cannot compare changes over time.

B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
b4 <- ggplot(b4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(b4)

B1 shows the percentage of pitches resulting in strikes within each pitch type. B4 shows how much each pitch type contributes to all pitches that resulted in strikes. The results can differ because pitch types are not thrown equally often.
